section_summary: This section opens with detailed Spanish inventories of Japanese diplomatic and consular property in Lima, followed by the protocol and extensive French-language inventory for the transfer of Japanese archives and effects in Tehran. The remaining documents report or debate Allied custody, examination, storage, sale, and financing arrangements for Japanese official property in China, Ireland, Denmark, Belgium, Morocco, Argentina, and Mexico. Several files reveal disagreements over policy—especially whether archives should be sent to Washington, whether movable property should be stored or sold, and how firmly to compel former Japanese officials to surrender records and assets.

subfiles.title: Continuation of List I: Inventory of Japanese Legation, Consulate, Residence, and Chancery Property in Lima
subfiles.from: Japanese Legation and Consulate in Lima
subfiles.about: Continues a numbered Spanish-language inventory of furniture, appliances, office equipment, films, books, and other property belonging to Japanese diplomatic and consular establishments in Lima.
subfiles.summary: The continuation completes the inventory of one residence and then separately lists the consul’s residence and chancery. It records household furniture, rugs, appliances, typewriters, cinematographic machines, Japanese films, office fittings, and sixty-six boxes or crates of miscellaneous articles. The inventory is dated at Lima on November 8, 1945.

subfiles.title: List II: Property Available to the Swedish Legation for Routine Protection Work
subfiles.about: Lists Japanese furniture and equipment placed at the Swedish Legation’s disposal for routine work connected with the protection of Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: List II dated November 8, 1945: household, garden and office items kept for Swedish protection work in Lima, including desks, rugs, typewriters and steel cabinets.

subfiles.title: Inventory of Boxes and Crates Belonging to the Japanese Legation and Consulate
subfiles.from: Japanese Legation and Consulate in Lima
subfiles.about: Describes the contents and ownership of numbered boxes and crates belonging to the Japanese Legation, Consulate, and individual Japanese officials.
subfiles.summary: Inventory of Japanese Legation and Consulate crates: stationery, seals, silver, records of the 1940 looting of Japanese property in Peru, civil-registration files, consular documents, crates belonging to named staff, and Red Cross insignia.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Beirut Regarding Japanese Archives
subfiles.about: Raises policy questions that must be decided before instructions can be drafted concerning Japanese archives in Lebanon.
subfiles.summary: Wadsworth will draft the Beirut instruction but recommends against French participation in the Allied committee unless France joins similar committees elsewhere, since the U.S., Soviet Union, Britain and China were Japan's victors; he asks whether they should join France on German archives.

subfiles.title: Chungking Telegram on Taking Over Japanese Archives in China
subfiles.about: Reports Chinese Foreign Office arrangements for assuming custody of Japanese diplomatic and consular archives and property.
subfiles.summary: Chungking: special representatives go to Shanghai, Nanking and Tientsin and local officials elsewhere; other Allies get access after inventories, finishing by end of January in Shanghai and Nanking but later where Japanese troops remain armed; no British or Soviet request yet.

subfiles.title: Dublin Telegram on the Japanese Consul General’s Continued Refusal
subfiles.about: Reports that the Japanese consul general continued to reject Allied instructions for surrendering consular archives and property.
subfiles.summary: Dublin: Japan's consul general again refuses the local Allied instruction as exceeding Tokyo's orders, demands to see American instructions and objects to "former"; the legation recommends a firm order, suspending his funds, and bankbooks for verification.

subfiles.title: Borton Memorandum Proposing an Addition to the Property Policy
subfiles.from: Hugh Borton, Division of Japanese Affairs
subfiles.about: Proposes language allowing the sale of Japanese government property when storage is impracticable while protecting officials’ private property from sale.
subfiles.summary: Borton proposes adding that Japanese government property may be sold if storage is impracticable, with proceeds into a trust account, but officials' private property not sold.

subfiles.title: Special Projects Division Memorandum on Storage or Sale of Japanese Property
subfiles.to: LE, JK, JA, and FE divisions
subfiles.about: Requests interdivisional views on a general policy for storing or disposing of Japanese diplomatic and consular property.
subfiles.summary: Special Projects recommends storing official Japanese property unless quantity, space or deterioration makes it impracticable, since Japan still has a government and the October 25 directive calls for custody, not liquidation; comments allow sale of government property but not officials' private goods.

subfiles.title: Duplicate Memorandum on Storage or Sale of Japanese Property
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of the proposal for a uniform policy governing Japanese diplomatic and consular property.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate memorandum: store Japanese property normally, with exceptions for excess, space, depreciation or deterioration; sale proceeds may be deposited; it argues against general liquidation and seeks regional divisions' views.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 174: Transfer of Japanese Archives and Property in Tehran
subfiles.from: Robert Rossow, Jr., for the United States ambassador in Tehran
subfiles.about: Reports the joint Allied transfer of Japanese diplomatic property and archives from Swedish custody to sealed storage in the former German Legation.
subfiles.summary: Tehran Despatch 174: China, Britain, the Soviet Union, the U.S. and Sweden moved Japanese material from a rented basement to the German Legation's, sealed November 30 with protocol and inventory; Aldrich wants intelligence examination, and the embassy suggests central shipment to avoid Soviet complications.

subfiles.title: Tehran Protocol Acknowledging Delivery of Japanese Property and Archives
subfiles.from: Representatives of the United States, China, Great Britain, and the Soviet Union in Tehran
subfiles.about: Formally acknowledges Allied receipt from Sweden of Japanese diplomatic and consular property and archives listed in an annex.
subfiles.summary: Tehran protocol, November 30, 1945: the Swedish Legation transfers Japanese property and archives to the four Allied powers' representatives; signed by Blake, Achourov, Chen Hou-Yu and the British representative.

subfiles.title: Annexed Inventory of Japanese Diplomatic and Consular Property in Tehran
subfiles.to: Representatives of the United States, Great Britain, China, and the Soviet Union
subfiles.about: Provides a detailed French-language inventory of Japanese archives, furniture, equipment, household goods, weapons, vehicles, art, tableware, and boxed effects transferred in Tehran.
subfiles.summary: The inventory begins with locked safes, filing cabinets, boxes of chancery records, books, office furniture, printing machines, firearms, rugs, and household furnishings. It continues through a motorcycle, radios, cameras, typewriters, Japanese artworks, silver, porcelain services, glassware, cutlery, kitchen equipment, preserved foods, clothing, and game tables. Conditions are carefully noted, including moth, damp, breakage, missing parts, and repairs performed after prolonged storage in a humid room.

subfiles.title: British Embassy Letter Transmitting Foreign Office Views
subfiles.from: G. R. Ranken, British Embassy, Washington
subfiles.to: A. W. Clattenburg, Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits British Foreign Office guidance on Japanese official archives and property in the Western Hemisphere.
subfiles.summary: Ranken forwards an extract of instructions to British Western Hemisphere missions, clarifying it covers Japanese archives in accredited countries, not U.S. territory, and offers to discuss.

subfiles.title: Extract from Foreign Office Telegram to British Missions in Latin America
subfiles.to: British diplomatic missions in Latin American countries
subfiles.about: Sets out British proposals for transporting Japanese archives, disposing of property, and funding the continued protection of Japanese nationals.
subfiles.summary: Foreign Office telegram: it favors shipping archives to Washington with unrestricted British access, ending leases, selling Japanese buildings and movable property except archives, stamps and seals, with proceeds in a joint account and funds kept for Japanese nationals' protection.

subfiles.title: Department of State Reply to Ranken on Divergent American Policy
subfiles.about: Explains revised American policy favoring traveling examination teams, storage of movable property, and jointly controlled trustee accounts.
subfiles.summary: State replies it no longer routinely plans to move Latin American archives to Washington, expecting local expert examination, favors storing movable official property and not selling officials' private property, and wants Japanese funds in a joint trustee account for protecting-power costs.

subfiles.title: Buenos Aires Airgram Requesting Authority to Dispose of Property
subfiles.about: Requests authority to dispose of Japanese property not needed in Argentina because storage space is a serious problem.
subfiles.summary: Buenos Aires: the British got authority to dispose of unnecessary Japanese Legation property; Cabot asks the same because storage takes considerable space.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 974: Custody of Japanese Property and Archives in Belgium
subfiles.about: Reports progress toward joint Four-Power custody and inventory of Japanese diplomatic and consular property in Belgium.
subfiles.summary: Belgium accepted replacing Sweden as custodian; representatives began inventorying the Japanese Embassy at Brussels, including Antwerp consulate material, and planned to seal documents; Patterson asks how caretaker, repair and heating costs are paid and reports Soviet interest in buying or renting the building.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2067: Further Refusal of the Japanese Consul General in Dublin
subfiles.about: Forwards correspondence documenting the Japanese consul general’s continued resistance to Allied surrender instructions.
subfiles.summary: Dublin: Japan's consul general still won't accept local American and British authority despite surrender and Tokyo's orders, claims equal standing and resists information demands; Gray and the British representative ask Allied headquarters to order cooperation.

subfiles.title: Japanese Consulate-General Cover Note Forwarding the December 3 Memorandum
subfiles.about: Forwards a memorandum concerning surrender of consular archives and property and the return of Japanese consular officers to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Japanese consulate-general cover note sends the American minister its December 3 memorandum, drawing attention to the translated instruction on notifying American and British representatives.

subfiles.title: Japanese Memorandum on Surrender and Repatriation
subfiles.from: Kazuo Ichihashi for the Japanese Consulate-General, Dublin
subfiles.about: Offers to deliver the official archives and property listed in an earlier inventory and requests travel arrangements for Japanese consular personnel.
subfiles.summary: Japanese memorandum cites urgent Foreign Office instructions to complete surrender, says property, archives and keys are ready for delivery where the Allies designate, and requests facilities for Consul General Setsuya Beppu, Mrs. Beppu and Consul Ichihashi to travel to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Annex I Cross-Reference to the Memorandum of November 12
subfiles.about: Identifies Annex I as a repetition of the Japanese Consulate-General’s November 12 memorandum already transmitted in an earlier despatch.
subfiles.summary: Annex I cross-reference: it repeats the November 12 memorandum earlier enclosed with Despatch 2055 of November 14.

subfiles.title: Annex II: Translation of Urgent Instructions from Tokyo
subfiles.from: Japanese Foreign Office, transmitting an Allied Headquarters directive
subfiles.about: Orders the consul general to obey the Allied representative’s directions for immediate surrender and notify the American and British representatives.
subfiles.summary: Annex II translates Tokyo's urgent instructions of November 26: the consul general must report at once to the American Consulate-General, deliver archives, property and keys, and notify the American and British representatives.

subfiles.title: McEnelly Letter Reporting Beppu’s Unannounced Visit
subfiles.from: Thomas McEnelly, American Consul General, Dublin
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese consul general’s delivery of a memorandum and asks for instructions before taking further action.
subfiles.summary: McEnelly says Setsuya Beppu appeared unannounced and left a communication signed by a subordinate; he told Colladay, copied Braddock, noted Beppu still hadn't complied with the November 10 Allied memorandum, and awaits Gray's instructions.

subfiles.title: McEnelly Letter Reporting the Japanese Consul General’s Refusal
subfiles.from: Thomas McEnelly, American Consul General, Dublin
subfiles.about: Describes Beppu’s refusal to accept a renewed American-British order to comply with the November surrender demands.
subfiles.summary: McEnelly summoned Beppu, who refused the communication as exceeding Tokyo's instructions, demanded to see American authority and objected to "former" consul general; the rejected instruction is enclosed.

subfiles.title: Joint American-British Instruction to the Former Japanese Consul General
subfiles.from: Thomas McEnelly and Geoffrey F. Braddock
subfiles.to: Former Japanese Consul General in Dublin
subfiles.about: Directs the former Japanese consul general to comply with the November 10 memorandum and appear with the requested records, articles, and information.
subfiles.summary: Joint American-British instruction returns the rejected memorandum and orders the consul general to comply and appear at the American Consulate-General December 5 at 3:30 p.m. with all documents, property and information; signed by McEnelly and Braddock.

subfiles.title: Japanese Memorandum Following the December 4 Conversations
subfiles.about: Restates the consulate’s willingness to surrender property under directions it considers consistent with Tokyo’s wording and asks how repatriation expenses will be paid.
subfiles.summary: Japanese memorandum: the consulate will deliver everything on directions conforming to Tokyo's instruction, insists on physical delivery, not just sealing, and asks who pays return personnel's travel costs.

subfiles.title: Correction to the Japanese Memorandum of December 5
subfiles.about: Corrects the date of the previous Japanese memorandum cited in the December 5 submission.
subfiles.summary: Correction slip dated December 6, 1945: the memorandum referenced on page one should be dated December 3, not December 4.

subfiles.title: Departmental Distribution of Despatch No. 2067
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Transmits the Dublin despatch on the Japanese consul general’s refusal to United States intelligence and law-enforcement agencies.
subfiles.summary: State forwards confidential Despatch 2067 from Dublin, on the consul general's refusal to obey surrender orders, to military and naval intelligence and the FBI.

subfiles.title: Copenhagen Airgram on Japanese Archives and Automobiles in Denmark
subfiles.about: Reports that Denmark held no Japanese archives but that two vehicles associated with the Japanese Naval Bureau in Berlin were in British military custody.
subfiles.summary: Copenhagen: no Japanese archives found; a Buick and Mercedes-Benz brought into Denmark for the Japanese Naval Bureau were seized as war material and used by the British, apparently Denmark's only Japanese property.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Madrid Concerning Japanese Material in Casablanca
subfiles.about: Authorizes French assumption of custody over Japanese archives and property held by the Spanish consul in Casablanca.
subfiles.summary: State tells Madrid French custody of Japanese material in Casablanca would accord with MacArthur's directive paragraph 1(B), assuming Madrid hadn't asked for joint American, British and French access; copy to Tangier.

subfiles.title: Madrid Airgram Asking Who Should Receive Japanese Material in Casablanca
subfiles.about: Asks whether Japanese archives and property held by the Spanish consul at Casablanca should be requested and transferred to French custody.
subfiles.summary: Madrid asks, invoking paragraph 1(B) of the October circular, whether the Casablanca Japanese material should be requested from the Spanish consul and given to the French; copy to Tangier.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 27,641: Disposition of Japanese Archives and Property in Mexico
subfiles.from: George S. Messersmith, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports Four-Power discussions in Mexico and requests clarification of American policy in light of British instructions.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith reports a December 4 meeting with British, Chinese and Soviet representatives after Sweden's notes to Mexico; the Soviet took a difficult position, the group will seek the Swedish minister's accounting, and he asks whether the U.S. concurs with Britain's policy of shipping archives to Washington and selling property.

subfiles.title: Geist Memorandum of the Four-Power Meeting in Mexico City
subfiles.about: Records negotiations among American, British, Chinese, and Soviet representatives over obtaining information about Japanese assets held by Sweden.
subfiles.summary: At the Mexico City meeting, Messersmith says Mexico doesn't object to transfer to the four powers; British and Chinese favor moving archives to Washington, Yakubovski demanded copies and assurances; they agreed Messersmith will request detailed asset information and Sweden will reply to each power.

subfiles.title: British Ambassador’s Letter on Disposal Policy in Mexico
subfiles.from: C. H. Bateman, British Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Provides British proposals for archives, property, funds, and protection work in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Bateman favors moving archives to Washington with British access, ending leases, selling Japanese buildings and movable property except records, stamps and seals, proceeds jointly administered, with Sweden retaining funds for Japanese nationals; he expects difficulty over the Swedish minister's funds.

subfiles.title: Messersmith’s Request for a Detailed Japanese Asset Statement
subfiles.about: Requests a quadruplicate accounting of all Japanese archives, property, liquid assets, obligations, and leases held by Sweden in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith, for the Four-Power representatives, asks the Swedish minister for descriptions and locations of Japanese archives, property, assets, accounts, obligations and leases, with separate copies for each power.

subfiles.title: Swedish Legation Note to the Mexican Foreign Office
subfiles.from: C. H. Petersén, Swedish chargé d’affaires ad interim
subfiles.to: Francisco Castillo Nájera, Mexican secretary of foreign relations
subfiles.about: Notifies Mexico that Sweden has been instructed to transfer Japanese diplomatic and consular property, funds, and archives to Allied representatives while continuing routine protection work.
subfiles.summary: Swedish Legation tells Mexico Japan asked Sweden to hand over Japanese property, funds and archives promptly; Sweden will deliver them to a jointly chosen representative of the U.S., Britain, China and the Soviets and keep routine matters for Japanese nationals.

subfiles.title: Mexican Foreign Office Reply to the Swedish Legation
subfiles.from: Francisco Castillo Nájera, Mexican Foreign Office
subfiles.to: Carl Henrik Gustaf Petersén, Swedish chargé d’affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Sweden’s notice of the proposed transfer of Japanese assets and its continued protection of Japanese nationals in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Mexico's Foreign Office recapitulates Sweden's plan to transfer Japanese property, funds and archives to the four powers' representatives and continue routine protection; Castillo Najera acknowledges receipt without objection.
